## &nbsp; {.dark .mid background-color="#1C242B"}

:::: {.vcenter}
::: {.statement}
A conference is not a reward<br>for work already finished.
:::

::: {.statement-hi}
It is an instrument you deploy<br>to answer a question.
:::

::: {.note}
Everything in the next fifty minutes follows from this one sentence.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**[00:00 – 00:03] · THE THESIS**

**SAY —**

"Before anything else, one sentence.

A conference is not a reward for work already finished."

*[ pause — do not fill it ]*

"It is an instrument you deploy to answer a question.

Most of us were taught the first version. You finish something, your advisor is pleased, you get sent somewhere. The trip is the prize. That framing is exactly why so many trips produce a certificate, a folder of photographs, and nothing else.

I want you to think about it the way you think about a characterization technique. You do not run XAS because you deserve it. You run it because there is something you cannot see any other way."

**DO —** Show of hands: who is presenting somewhere in the next twelve months? Note roughly how many — you will use it at the end.
:::

## Fifty minutes, five parts {.tint background-color="#F3F0EB"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Today
:::

::: {.agenda}
- [4 min]{.chip .c-teal} Why a conference is an instrument
- [8 min]{.chip .c-teal} Choosing the right meeting
- [8 min]{.chip .c-teal} The months before you travel
- [10 min]{.chip .c-amber} Designing the talk and the poster
- [9 min]{.chip .c-amber} Handling questions in English
- [6 min]{.chip .c-teal} The first 48 hours after you return
- [10 min]{.chip .c-slate} Questions
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
Interrupt earlier if something is unclear. The last ten minutes are yours either way.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:03 – 00:04] · AGENDA**

**SAY —**

"This is the shape of the hour. Five parts, then ten minutes for your questions.

Two of these are the ones people skip — part two, what you do in the months before, and part five, what you do in the two days after. Those are also where almost all of the value is. The parts everyone prepares for, the talk and the poster, matter less than you think."

**DO —** Do not explain the five parts here. Each gets its own section.
:::

## Three questions a laboratory cannot answer

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Why this is an instrument
:::

::: {.cards .feature}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[]{.dot}

### Is the question still open?

Whether someone across the world solved your problem eight months ago and has not published it yet.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### Does the argument survive contact?

Whether your interpretation holds when a stranger who has no reason to be kind attacks it.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[]{.dot}

### Who would work with you?

Which people have the instrument, the sample, or the model you are missing — and would say yes.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
If a meeting cannot answer at least one of these for the work you have right now, it is tourism.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:04 – 00:08] · THE ARGUMENT**

**SAY —**

"Three things you cannot get in the laboratory, no matter how good your equipment is.

First: the state of the unpublished field. Literature tells you what was true eighteen months ago. A conference tells you what three groups are doing right now and have not written up. That difference has killed projects in this department.

Second: adversarial review. Your advisor is on your side. Your co-authors are invested. At a conference someone who has never met you, and who does not care about your feelings, tells you where the argument leaks. That is worth more than a month of polishing.

Third: access to capability you do not own. Every collaboration this group has started began as a conversation next to a poster, not as an email."

*[ deliver the closing line lightly, then move on ]*

"So if a meeting cannot answer at least one of these for the work you have on your bench right now — go if you enjoy it. But do not call it research."

**DO —** Do not lecture on the closing line. Land it and change slide.
:::

## Choosing the right meeting {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 1 · 8 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Match the venue to the stage the work is at, not to the prestige you would like.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:08] · SECTION BREAK**

**SAY —** "The first mistake happens months before the trip, when you choose the wrong meeting."

**DO —** Give the failure mode from our own group without naming anyone: three months of preliminary data, applies to the largest meeting in the field, gets a poster in a hall of nine hundred posters, speaks to four people, comes home believing conferences are useless.
:::

## Three stages, three kinds of meeting

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 1
:::

::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card .c-sky}
[Early]{.eyebrow}

### An idea and a trend

Domestic or regional meeting, small session. The goal is criticism, not visibility — you want the awkward question now, while the design can still change.

**Take the poster.** Thirty minutes per person beats three.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[Middle]{.eyebrow}

### A result you believe

Specialist international meeting in your subfield. The goal is to test the interpretation against people who know the system as well as you do.

**Fight for the oral slot.** This is where collaborations start.
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[Late]{.eyebrow}

### A paper near submission

Large flagship meeting, or an invited talk. The goal is priority, visibility, and reviewer familiarity.

**Least useful for improving the work.** It is already fixed.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
One question decides it: what would have to happen at this meeting for the trip to have been worth it?
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:08 – 00:13] · MATCHING STAGE TO VENUE**

**SAY —**

"Three stages of a piece of work, three different meetings.

Early — you have an idea and a trend, not a result. You want a small meeting where you will be criticized. And take the poster.

I know a poster feels like a demotion. It is not. A talk gives you three minutes of questions from people who are half asleep after lunch. A poster gives you an hour of one-to-one conversation with exactly the people who chose to stop and read it. At the early stage the poster is strictly the better instrument.

Middle — you have a result you believe. Now you want the specialist meeting, and now the oral slot is worth fighting for, because you want the people who know your system to attack your interpretation.

Late — the paper is nearly submitted. Big meeting, visibility, priority. Be honest with yourself that this one will not improve the work. The argument is already fixed."

**DO —** Spend most of the section on the middle column; that is where this audience sits. Put the closing question on the board and tell them to write it in their notebook.
:::

## Reading a meeting before you commit

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 1
:::

::: {.numbered .n4}
1. **Who chairs the sessions?** Look at the symposium organizers, not the plenary list. Organizers decide who is in the room.
2. **Where does the abstract end up?** Reviewed abstract, full proceedings paper, or nothing? This decides whether the work is still publishable later.
3. **Who came last time?** Find last year's programme. If the three groups you cite most are absent, it is the wrong meeting.
4. **What is the cost per useful contact?** Registration plus travel, divided by the number of people you realistically expect to talk to.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.flag}
Warning signs — an invitation email that flatters you · a scope covering five unrelated fields · a fee due before review · a venue that changes city every year · no named programme committee
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:13 – 00:16] · DUE DILIGENCE**

**SAY —**

"Four checks, none of which takes more than ten minutes.

Number two is the one that has actually cost people in this department. Some meetings publish a full proceedings paper. Several journals treat that as prior publication. Check your target journal's policy before you agree to a full paper, not after.

Number three is the cheapest and the most reliable. Last year's programme is public. Open it and search for the three groups you cite most. If none of them is there, this is not your meeting, whatever it is called."

**DO —** On the warning signs: say plainly that these invitations arrive weekly, that they are written to flatter, and that accepting costs money and reputation. Tell them to forward anything they are unsure about to you.
:::

## The months before you travel {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 2 · 8 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Everything that decides the value of the trip is decided before you board.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:16] · SECTION BREAK**

**SAY —** "You have chosen the meeting. From here the clock runs backward from the abstract deadline, not forward from today."
:::

## Plan backward from the abstract deadline

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 2
:::

::: {.steps}
::: {.step .c-teal}
[T−6 months]{.n}
[Decide the claim]{.h}
[Name the one sentence you intend to defend. Identify the experiment still missing to support it.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-sky}
[T−4 months]{.n}
[Close the data gap]{.h}
[Run the missing measurement. Assume one repeat will fail, and budget for it.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-amber}
[T−3 months]{.n}
[Submit the abstract]{.h}
[Promise the result you will have. Not the topic you are working on.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-sage}
[T−6 weeks]{.n}
[Build the materials]{.h}
[Figures at final quality. Draft slides or poster. Travel booked, paperwork started.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-rust}
[T−2 weeks]{.n}
[Rehearse and target]{.h}
[Two full rehearsals with questions. Write down the people and sessions you are going for.]{.d}
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
The abstract is a contract, not a title. "The effect of X on Y was investigated" tells the committee you do not yet know what you found.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:16 – 00:21] · BACKWARD PLANNING**

**SAY —**

"Copy this timeline. It is the practical core of the whole hour.

The step people get wrong is T−3. You submit a topic instead of a claim, because the data are not in yet. And that is honest — but the fix is not at T−3, it is at T−6. If you decide at six months out which single claim you are going for, then at three months out you can promise it truthfully.

Compare these two abstracts. 'The effect of electrolyte additive on zinc anodes was investigated.' Versus: 'A two weight per cent additive suppresses dendrite nucleation and triples cycle life at five milliamps per square centimetre, and we show why.'

The first one is accepted as a poster. The second one is accepted as a talk."

**DO —** Mention the local reality: leave request, funding approval, and visa each take longer than students expect, and the paperwork sits at T−6 weeks for a reason.
:::

## Four things to have ready before you fly

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 2
:::

::: {.cards .stack .numbered-stack}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[1]{.numdot}

### A 30-second introduction

Who you are, which group, what problem you work on. Rehearsed until it bores you. You will use it forty times.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[2]{.numdot}

### A 2-minute version of the work

Question, approach, key result, why it matters. No slides. This is what you say standing next to a coffee urn.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[3]{.numdot}

### A one-page summary to leave behind

Title, one figure, three results, your email, a QR code to the preprint. People lose business cards; they keep paper with a figure on it.
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[4]{.numdot}

### A named target list

Five people you want to meet. Three sessions you will not miss. One question you want answered. Written down, on your phone.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:21 – 00:24] · WHAT TO CARRY**

**SAY —**

"Four things. None of them is a slide deck.

Number one, done badly: 'I am a master student at Chula and I work on batteries.' Nobody can do anything with that.

Done properly: 'I am a master student in Chemical Engineering at Chulalongkorn — I work on why zinc anodes fail in the first fifty cycles rather than the last.' Now the person in front of you either knows something about that or knows who does.

Number four is what separates a productive trip from a passive one. And email one or two of those five people before you travel. One short paragraph: who you are, what you will present, could they spare ten minutes. The hit rate is much higher than you expect, because almost nobody does it."

**DO —** Read the abstract book on the flight out, not in the taxi home. Say that line and let it sit.
:::

## Designing for the time you are given {.dark .divider .c-amber background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 3 · 10 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
A twelve-minute talk is not a short seminar. A poster is not a paper on a wall.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:24] · SECTION BREAK**

**SAY —** "The two formats fail in opposite directions. Talks fail by being too full. Posters fail by being unreadable from two metres."
:::

## Anatomy of a 12 + 3 talk

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 3
:::

::: {.dots}
- **2 min · Why should anyone care?** The problem, in the audience's language. One sentence they could repeat at dinner.
- **3 min · What exactly did you do?** Enough method for a stranger to believe the data. Not the full protocol.
- **5 min · What did you find?** The core. Two or three figures, each with one message said out loud.
- **2 min · What does it mean?** Interpretation, the honest limitation, and the one thing you would do next.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
One message per slide, written as the slide title · about one slide per minute · memorize only the first 60 seconds and the last 30 · finish 30 seconds early
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:24 – 00:29] · TALK STRUCTURE**

**SAY —**

"Twelve minutes and three for questions. Here is where the twelve go.

Look at the split. Results get five minutes, method gets three. Most student talks invert that — six minutes on the experimental setup and ninety seconds on what was found. You are not being judged on how carefully you worked. You are being judged on whether the claim is warranted.

On memorizing: only the opening sixty seconds and the closing thirty. Those are the two places where attention is highest and a stumble is expensive. The middle you speak freely from your own figures, because you know them better than anyone in the room.

And finish thirty seconds early. Every session chair in the world is running late by mid-afternoon. Nobody has ever resented a speaker who gave them time back — and chairs remember who did."

**DO —** If anyone says "I know this is hard to read", stop them. The instruction is to remove the slide, not to apologize for it.
:::

## A poster is read at three distances

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 3
:::

::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card .c-teal}
[3 m]{.big}

### The title does the work

Three seconds, while walking past. Write the finding, not the topic. *"Additive X triples zinc anode life"* stops people. *"A study of additives for zinc anodes"* does not.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[1 m]{.big}

### One figure carries the claim

A visitor who stops gives you thirty seconds of silent reading. One large central figure, labelled so it works without you standing beside it.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[arm's length]{.big}

### The detail is there if asked

Method, conditions and controls in small type at the edges. Present for the specialist, invisible to everyone else.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.flag}
Stand beside your poster, not in front of it · open with "May I give you the two-minute version?" · put your name and email large enough to photograph
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:29 – 00:34] · POSTER DESIGN**

**SAY —**

"Three distances. If you remember one thing from this slide, it is the first one.

Your title is the only part of your poster that most people will ever read. So it must state a finding. Not a topic, not a method, not a system — a finding, in ordinary words, that someone can disagree with.

The behaviour matters as much as the design. Standing in front of your own poster blocks it. Stand to the side. And do not wait to be asked — when someone slows down, offer the two-minute version. Most people are relieved."

**DO —** If time allows, ask for one real poster title from the room and rewrite it live. That lands far harder than my example. Keep it to two, then move on.
:::

## Handling questions in English {.dark .divider .c-amber background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 4 · 9 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
Nobody in that room is grading your grammar. They are watching how you think.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:34] · SECTION BREAK**

**SAY —** "This is the part most of you are actually worried about, so let us name it. Fluency is not the requirement. Being understood is the requirement — and being understood is mostly structure and speed, not vocabulary."
:::

## Almost every question is one of five

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 4
:::

::: {.cards .g3 .wrap}
::: {.card .c-sky}
[1]{.numdot}

### Clarification

*"What was the scan rate?"* Easy. Answer in one sentence and stop talking.
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[2]{.numdot}

### Challenge to the method

*"How do you know it is not an artefact?"* Name the control you ran — or concede that you have not run it.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[3]{.numdot}

### Alternative explanation

*"Could this be X instead?"* Often the most useful question you will get. Say what evidence would separate the two.
:::

::: {.card .c-rust}
[4]{.numdot}

### Scope and generality

*"Does this work for other systems?"* Answer where the boundary is, not a hopeful yes.
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[5]{.numdot}

### "Have you seen my paper?"

Rarely hostile. Thank them, write the reference down where they can see you do it, and mean it.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:34 – 00:38] · THE FIVE TYPES**

**SAY —**

"In fifteen years of sessions I have not heard a question that was not one of these five.

Type three deserves your attention. Somebody standing up and saying 'could this be something else?' has just given you a reviewer comment, free, months before you submit. The wrong response is to defend. The right response is: here is the measurement that would distinguish the two possibilities — and if you have not done it, say so.

Type five is usually a senior person who would like to be cited. Writing the reference down in front of them is worth more than any answer you could give."

**DO —** Prepare one answer for each type before you travel. You are not predicting the question. You are removing the panic.
:::

## One structure for every answer

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 4
:::

::: {.steps}
::: {.step .c-teal}
[1]{.n}
[Acknowledge]{.h}
["Thank you, that is an important point." Buys three seconds and costs nothing.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-amber}
[2]{.n}
[Restate]{.h}
["So you are asking whether the capacity loss comes from the anode rather than the electrolyte?" Lets them correct you cheaply.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-rust}
[3]{.n}
[Answer in one sentence]{.h}
[The direct answer first. Not the background, not the history.]{.d}
:::

::: {.step .c-sage}
[4]{.n}
[Offer the detail]{.h}
["I can show the control experiment if that is useful." Let them choose to go deeper.]{.d}
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.note}
*"Could you repeat the question, please?"* · *"I want to make sure I understood — do you mean …?"* · *"I do not know. What would settle it is …"* · *"That is a fair criticism, and here is what we did about it."* · *"Could we continue this at the coffee break?"*
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:38 – 00:43] · THE ANSWER STRUCTURE**

**SAY —**

"Four steps, in this order, for every question you will ever be asked.

Step two is the one that saves you. Restating the question does three things at once: it proves you heard it, it gives the asker a cheap chance to correct you before you answer the wrong question, and it buys you five seconds of thinking time that looks like courtesy rather than hesitation.

The most important line on this slide is 'I do not know.' Saying it costs you nothing. Pretending costs you the room for the rest of the session. And notice what follows it — 'what would settle it is' — that turns an admission into a research statement.

One more thing, and it is the one nobody tells you: slow down. Under stress, non-native speakers speed up. That is exactly backwards. Speak slowly and stop at the end of the sentence."

**DO —** Demonstrate it. Ask a volunteer to throw a hostile question at their own work, then answer it in front of the room using all four steps. The demonstration is worth more than the slide.
:::

## The first 48 hours after you return {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Part 5 · 6 minutes
:::

::: {.lede}
This is where most conference value is lost — quietly, and permanently.
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:43] · SECTION BREAK**

**SAY —** "Be honest about the conditions. You will be tired, there will be four hundred emails, and there will be a class you missed. If you do nothing in the first two days, the trip converts itself into a certificate."
:::

## Convert the trip before it evaporates

::: {.kicker .c-teal}
Part 5
:::

::: {.cards .stack}
::: {.card .c-sky}
[]{.dot}

### Before you land

Write the trip note. Two pages on the plane, while it is fresh: what you learned, who you met, what changed in your plan.
:::

::: {.card .c-sage}
[]{.dot}

### Within 24 hours

Send the follow-ups. Three sentences each: where we met, what we discussed, what I propose next. Attach the one-pager. After a week they no longer remember your face.
:::

::: {.card .c-amber}
[]{.dot}

### Within 48 hours

Turn questions into work. Every question you could not answer becomes an experiment, a control, a paper to read, or a paragraph to rewrite.
:::

::: {.card .c-teal}
[]{.dot}

### Within a week

Report back to the group. Fifteen minutes at group meeting is how one funded trip becomes useful to twelve people.
:::
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.punch}
Send the follow-up emails from the airport. Waiting until you feel rested means waiting until it is too late.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:43 – 00:47] · CLOSING THE LOOP**

**SAY —**

"Four things, and none of them takes an afternoon.

The trip note is not bureaucracy. It is the only durable record that will exist. Most of what you learned at a conference is gone within two weeks and written down nowhere — and then next year somebody in this group repeats an experiment that a stranger told you had already failed.

The follow-up email is three sentences. Where we met, what we discussed, what I propose next. That is all. The reason it must go within a day is that the person met sixty people that week, and your face has a shelf life.

And report back at group meeting. That is partly generosity and partly self-interest: it is also how you justify the next trip."

**DO —** Tell them the trip note template lives with the handout, and that you will read anyone's if they want a second pair of eyes.
:::

## Judge the trip by what changed {.dark background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
If you remember three things
:::

::: {.numbered .n3}
1. **Choose on purpose** The meeting must match the stage the work is at. Prestige is not a criterion.
2. **Design for the time you are given** Twelve minutes, one message per slide. Three metres, a title that states a finding.
3. **Close the loop within 48 hours** Trip note, follow-up emails, questions turned into experiments.
:::

::: {.foot}
::: {.statement-sub}
A conference is a research instrument. Before the next one you attend, write down what you intend it to measure.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**[00:47 – 00:50] · CLOSE**

**SAY —**

"Three things, and then your questions.

Choose on purpose. Design for the time you are given. Close the loop within forty-eight hours.

And the sentence we started with: a conference is a research instrument. So before the next one you attend, write down what you intend it to measure. If you cannot finish that sentence, you are not ready to book the flight.

Questions?"

**DO —**

- Do not summarize the summary. Stop and open the floor.
- If the room is silent, seed it: "who has a conference in the next six months, and what are you worried about?" That question always produces a real one.
- Close by offering to read a draft abstract for anyone who sends one at least three weeks before their deadline. Say the number — three weeks — or you will receive them the night before.
:::
